content: Genital candidiasis is a common fungal infection caused by the overgrowth of a fungus known as Candida. Candida is naturally present in the body in small amounts. However, when an imbalance occurs, such as changes in the normal acidity of the vagina or hormonal fluctuations, Candida can multiply excessively. This overgrowth leads to the development of symptoms associated with candidiasis. The primary species responsible for this condition is Candida albicans, although other species such as C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, and C. krusei can also be involved. In rare cases, other Candida species may contribute to the infection. Candidiasis is the fourth most common cause of nosocomial bloodstream infections. The incidence rate is approximately 8 cases per 100,000 individuals in the general population. The mortality rate associated with bloodstream and disseminated Candida infections is alarmingly high, approaching 50%. Invasive candidiasis is more likely to occur in critically ill patients, particularly those in intensive care units, individuals with severe granulocytopenia, and recipients of hematopoietic stem cell or organ transplants. Genital candidiasis is also associated with HIV infection. Vulvovaginal candidiasis is frequently linked to conditions such as pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, and the use of antibiotics. The treatment of vaginal yeast infections typically involves antifungal medications. These drugs can be administered orally, applied directly to the affected area, or used intravaginally. Antifungal therapy is generally effective, with a success rate of 80% to 90%. However, treatment-resistant infections are becoming increasingly common, particularly in women with HIV who are undergoing long-term antifungal therapy. Prolonged and frequent use of antifungal treatments can reduce their effectiveness over time.
